passage: Pallavi had been back in Pune from her exchange term in Utrecht for a week when she watched her classmate Jagdish invite her aunt to a birthday. "Maybe, we'll see," said her aunt with a warm smile. Jagdish nodded happily and said he would keep a chair. Pallavi bit her lip: at home a soft maybe is sometimes a gentle no. In Utrecht her host family had said, "No, I don't want to," straight out, and at first she had felt slapped. Now she saw that neither was rude in its own place. She quietly told Jagdish, "Maybe can be a kind way of saying no. You could ask her again another way." Jagdish laughed and thanked her.

qa.q: Where had Pallavi spent her exchange term?
qa.a: Pallavi spent her exchange term in Utrecht.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel when her aunt said maybe, and why?
qa.a: Uneasy and a little worried for Jagdish, because a warm maybe can be a gentle no, and Pallavi had just learned the bluntness abroad.

qa.q: How could Pallavi help Jagdish read both styles?
qa.a: By explaining that maybe can be a kind way of saying no and suggesting he ask again another way, without calling either style rude.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt hearing maybe, we'll see?
qa.a: Hopeful and happy, taking the warm smile as a likely yes.

grounding: A teenager on exchange notices direct and indirect refusals and sees neither is rude in its own setting.

passage:
In the school canteen in Auckland, Chinmay tried something new.
Chinmay: Nilesh, do you want to come to the night market with me tonight?
Nilesh: No, thanks. I'm going to stay in and finish my project.
Chinmay: Oh. Okay. (The smile slid for a second.)
Nilesh: What? Did I say something wrong?
Chinmay: At home a no usually comes wrapped in a maybe. Like, let me see.
Nilesh: Here, if I mean maybe I say maybe. If I mean no I say no. It isn't rude.
Chinmay: I'm starting to see that. So can I ask what you'd like to do on Saturday?
Nilesh: Saturday, yes! Table tennis?
Chinmay: Table tennis. And if you're tired, just tell me straight.
Nilesh: Deal.

qa.q: What plan did Nilesh give instead of going to the night market?
qa.a: Nilesh planned to stay in and finish the project.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel at first on hearing No, thanks?
qa.a: A little hurt or taken aback; the smile slid for a second.

qa.q: How did Chinmay handle the difference next?
qa.a: Chinmay asked Nilesh about Saturday and asked for straight answers when Nilesh is tired.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh say a no is not rude?
qa.a: Because in that place maybe means maybe and no means no, so being direct is honest, not unkind.

grounding: A teenager on exchange notices that a blunt no abroad differs from a softened maybe at home and learns to read both.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Looking back on my exchange term in Munich, the moment I, Yamini, remember most is the soup. My host mother, Frau Weber, asked if I wanted more, and I said, "Maybe a little," the way I'd say it at home, meaning yes please. She put the pot away. I was shocked. And when my host sister Lena didn't want to come to the cinema with me and Aditi, the other Indian student, she just said, "No, I don't feel like it." No maybe, no excuse. I felt slapped. Aditi and I talked about it for an hour on the tram. At home, my mother says "we'll see" when she means no. Here "no" meant only no, and it wasn't cold. Lena still made me tea. By the end I was saying "Yes, please" and "No, thanks" like them, and it felt strangely light.

qa.q: What did Yamini say when asked if she wanted more soup?
qa.a: "Maybe a little."

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when Lena said a plain no?
qa.a: Yamini felt slapped and hurt at first, because at home a refusal is usually softened.

qa.q: What helped Yamini learn to read both styles?
qa.a: Talking it over with Aditi and noticing that Lena was still kind after saying no, which showed a blunt no was not rude there.

qa.q: How might Lena have seen Yamini's reaction to her plain no?
qa.a: Lena probably didn't notice any rudeness in it, and might have been puzzled if Yamini seemed hurt, since for her no is just honest.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange noticing blunt refusals abroad and softened ones at home, and learning to read both.

passage:
Exchange coordinator's note, week 3, Utrecht programme.
Chetan asked to talk after the Tuesday session. He said his host mother, Sharmila, who moved to the Netherlands twenty years ago, and her Dutch husband keep saying no "straight to the face". When he offered to cook dinner, Sharmila said, "No, not tonight, I've planned something." When he asked to borrow the bicycle, the answer was "No, it has a flat tyre." Chetan said at home people would say "let's see" or "maybe tomorrow", and he'd been lying awake thinking the family didn't like him. He noticed Sharmila herself had changed; at an Indian dinner party she softened every refusal.
I explained that in this house a plain no is simply information, not a verdict. He laughed at himself a little. I suggested he ask Sharmila directly. He did, the same evening, and texted me: "She said she likes me a lot. Also she fixed the tyre."

qa.q: What reason did Sharmila give for saying no to the bicycle?
qa.a: "No, it has a flat tyre."

qa.q: How had Chetan been feeling about the family's plain answers?
qa.a: He had been anxious and hurt, lying awake thinking the family didn't like him.

qa.q: What did the coordinator suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To ask Sharmila directly, because a plain question matched the family's direct style and cleared up his worry the same evening.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see her own two ways of saying no?
qa.a: She probably moves between them without much thought, plain at home in Utrecht and softer at an Indian dinner party, and may have been surprised Chetan felt rejected.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange observing blunt refusals in his host family, contrasted with softened ones at home, and learning to read both.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Sunday night, Perth
Journal, today was weird. At the beach barbecue I asked Mia's dad if Saurabh could join us next weekend, and he said, "No, sorry, it's family only." Just that. Then he flipped a sausage like nothing happened. I stood there with my face burning. At home Papa would have said "we'll see, beta" and we'd all know it meant no, but softly.
Later Saurabh (who is staying with the Nguyens) said his host mum does the same. "Do you want dessert?" "No thanks." Done. He thinks it's efficient. I think it's a bit like being hit with a cushion. Not painful, just surprising.
But then Mia's dad asked me to choose the music for the car, as if nothing was wrong, because nothing was. Maybe here no is just no, and maybe at home maybe is also no. I'm learning two languages in English. Sarika, the translator.

qa.q: What did Mia's dad say when asked if Saurabh could join?
qa.a: "No, sorry, it's family only."

qa.q: How did Sarika feel when Mia's dad said no so plainly?
qa.a: Sarika was embarrassed and surprised, with a burning face, like being hit with a cushion.

qa.q: What is Sarika learning to do?
qa.a: Sarika is learning to read a blunt no as plain information here and a soft maybe as a no at home, without taking either as rude.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see the direct style?
qa.a: Saurabh sees it as efficient rather than rude, which helps Sarika think about it differently.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange noticing blunt refusals abroad and softened ones at home, and learning to read both as normal.

passage:
Varun: ok culture shock of the day. asked my host sister if she wanted to come to the football match with us. she said "No, I don't like football." just like that 😳
Arnab: harsh
Varun: that's what I thought! but she wasn't angry. she offered to make pancakes for when we got back
Arnab: at home that'd be "let's see, maybe, I'll try" 😅
Varun: and then they don't come. exactly. and here if they say maybe, it means they're actually not sure
Arnab: so which is ruder?
Varun: neither I think. here the plain no is honest, at home the maybe is being polite. I kept hearing rude when it wasn't
Arnab: so what did you do
Varun: said "no problem, pancakes sound great." she smiled. and I'm practising a clear no myself
Arnab: try it on me. come to my cousin's engagement Sunday?
Varun: ...I'll see 🙂

qa.q: What did Varun's host sister offer to make?
qa.a: She offered to make pancakes for when they got back.

qa.q: What did Varun feel when his host sister said no so plainly?
qa.a: Varun felt surprised and a bit stung at first, hearing it as harsh before seeing she wasn't angry.

qa.q: What is Varun learning to do?
qa.a: Varun is learning to read both styles, not hearing rudeness in a plain no, and practising giving a clear no too.

qa.q: How might the host sister see her own "No, I don't like football"?
qa.a: To her it was probably just honest and friendly, which is why she offered pancakes right after.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on an exchange who notices that people abroad say no bluntly while at home a no is softened, and learns that neither is rude in its own setting.
